alignment.note: μή / ܕܠܡܐ / ne — negative purpose particle 'lest'.

Greek uses a circumstantial aorist participle (ἐλθών, 'having come'); the Vulgate renders this with a finite temporal clause (cum venerit), while the Peshitta employs a finite verb (ܢܐܬܐ, 'he may come'). All express the same temporal-conditional notion but with differing syntactic structures.

Greek and Latin use a single adverb (ἐξαίφνης / repente, 'suddenly'); the Peshitta renders the sense with a prepositional phrase ܡܢ ܫܠܝܐ ('from quietness/stillness'), an idiomatic Syriac construction for sudden, unexpected action.

Greek εὕρῃ and Latin inveniat are independent subjunctive verbs governed by the purpose particle; the Peshitta coordinates the verb with a prefixed waw (ܘܢܫܟܚܟܘܢ, 'and he may find you'), fusing the pronominal object suffix into the verb.
ὑμᾶς / -ܟܘܢ (object suffix) / vos — second-person plural object.

Greek and Latin use a single present participle (καθεύδοντας / dormientes, 'sleeping'); the Peshitta expands this into a subordinate clause introduced by ܟܕ ('while') with a participle and an explicit independent pronoun (ܕܡܟܝܢ ܐܢܬܘܢ, 'while you are sleeping'), a typical Syriac periphrastic construction.
